content: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), including meclofenamate, may increase the risk of heart attack or stroke. These events can occur suddenly and may be fatal. The risk is higher for individuals who use NSAIDs for extended periods. Seek emergency medical attention immediately if you experience chest pain, shortness of breath, weakness on one side of the body, or slurred speech. Do not take meclofenamate before or after coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery. Meclofenamate and other NSAIDs can cause ulcers, bleeding, or perforations in the stomach or intestines. These complications can occur at any time during treatment, often without warning, and may be fatal. The risk is higher for individuals who use NSAIDs long-term, are older, have poor health, or consume large amounts of alcohol. Inform your doctor if you are taking anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin), aspirin, other NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen, naproxen), or oral steroids (e.g., prednisone, dexamethasone). Also, disclose if you have a history of ulcers, gastrointestinal bleeding, or other bleeding disorders. Stop taking meclofenamate and contact your doctor if you experience stomach pain, heartburn, vomiting blood or material resembling coffee grounds, blood in the stool, or black, tarry stools. Your doctor will monitor your condition closely and may order tests to evaluate your response to meclofenamate. It is important to communicate how you are feeling so your doctor can adjust your dosage to minimize the risk of serious side effects. Always read the medication guide provided by your doctor or pharmacist and ask questions if needed. You can also access the guide on the FDA website. Meclofenamate is prescribed to alleviate pain, tenderness, swelling, and stiffness associated with osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis. It is also used to treat mild to moderate pain, including menstrual pain, and to reduce heavy menstrual bleeding. This medication belongs to the NSAID class and works by inhibiting the production of substances in the body that cause pain, fever, and inflammation. Meclofenamate is available in capsule form and is typically taken three to four times daily for arthritis, three times daily for heavy menstrual bleeding, or every 4-6 hours as needed for pain. It can be taken with food or milk to prevent stomach upset. If taken regularly, it should be taken at the same times each day. Follow your prescription instructions carefully and do not alter the dosage without consulting your doctor. If you are using meclofenamate for heavy menstrual bleeding, contact your doctor if the bleeding does not decrease or if you experience spotting or bleeding between periods. For arthritis, symptom improvement may take several days, with full benefits potentially taking 2-3 weeks or longer. Meclofenamate may also be prescribed for conditions such as ankylosing spondylitis, gouty arthritis, and psoriatic arthritis. Discuss the risks and benefits of using this medication with your doctor. Before starting meclofenamate, inform your doctor if you are allergic to it, aspirin, other NSAIDs, or any of the inactive ingredients in the capsules. Provide a complete list of all medications, supplements, and herbal products you are taking, especially those mentioned in the warning section. Notify your doctor if you have a history of asthma, nasal polyps, swelling in the extremities, or liver or kidney disease. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. Meclofenamate should not be used during the last months of pregnancy. If you become pregnant while taking this medication, contact your doctor immediately. Inform your healthcare provider if you are scheduled for surgery, including dental procedures. Unless otherwise directed by your doctor, continue your normal diet while taking meclofenamate. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember, unless it is close to the time for your next dose. Do not double the dose to make up for a missed one. Common side effects of meclofenamate include diarrhea, constipation, gas, mouth sores, headache, and ringing in the ears. If these symptoms persist or worsen, inform your doctor. Serious side effects include blurred vision, unexplained weight gain, fever, blisters, rash, itching, hives, swelling, hoarseness, difficulty breathing or swallowing, yellowing of the skin or eyes, fatigue, unusual bleeding or bruising, loss of appetite, upper right abdominal pain, flu-like symptoms, pale skin, rapid heartbeat, discolored or bloody urine, back pain, and painful urination. Stop taking the medication and contact your doctor immediately if you experience any of these symptoms. Report serious side effects to the FDA's MedWatch program. Store meclofenamate in its original container, tightly sealed, at room temperature, away from heat and moisture. Keep it out of reach of children. Dispose of expired or unused medication properly, consulting your pharmacist if needed. In case of overdose, contact a poison control center at 1-800-222-1222 or call 911 if the individual has collapsed or is not breathing. Symptoms of overdose may include confusion, agitation, seizures, and reduced urination. Do not share this medication with others. Consult your pharmacist if you have questions about refilling your prescription.
